about: The epistola of the formulary “Quinquagesima Sunday” in the 1962 Roman Missal.

seg.tr: Brothers: If I speak in the tongues of men and angels but have no love, I have become like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal. And even if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and even if I have all faith so that I can move mountains, but have no love, I am nothing. And even if I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, and even if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but have no love, it profits me nothing. Love is patient and kind; love does not envy, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, does not seek prestige, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked, does not harbor evil thoughts, does not rejoice in iniquity, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Love never falls away: if there are prophecies, they will be made void; if there are tongues, they will cease; if there is knowledge, it will be destroyed. For we know in part and we prophesy in part. But when what is perfect comes, what is partial will be done away. When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child. But when I became a man, I put away what belonged to childhood. Now we see through a mirror, in an obscure manner, but then face to face. Now I know in part, but then I will know even as I have been known. But now faith, hope and love remain, these three; but the greatest of these is love.

a.g: I speak with the tongues of men
so that I can move mountains
does not seek its own interests
if there are prophecies, they will be made void
if there are tongues, they will cease
if there is knowledge, it will be destroyed
But when what is perfect comes
what is partial will be done away
even as I have been known
but the greatest of these is love

ex.w005: In the clause introduced by si, loquar can be present subjunctive or future indicative. Its pairing with habeam supports a hypothetical reading here. Factus sum remains Latin perfect indicative, presenting the resulting state.
ex.w022: Habuero is first-person future perfect: the possession precedes the envisaged consequence. English uses a present form in this conditional clause without changing the Latin tense or mood. Noverim, by contrast, is perfect subjunctive, expressing knowledge in this context.
ex.w133: The coming of what is perfect precedes the announced ending of what is partial. Venerit can be future perfect indicative or perfect subjunctive. The future context supports the former analysis, but the form alone does not decide the mood.
